DS-MizarAlcor.answer: Mizar, Alcor, Merak, Phecda, Megrez and Alioth very likely form one family, while Dubhe and Alkaid are strangers passing through. Merak, about two and a half times the Sun's mass, is among the family's heaviest survivors and still white, so the family clock has already claimed stars much heavier than that. Dubhe's orange, a giant's color, belongs to a stranger.
DS-MizarAlcor.story: Membership is tested the way you would pick out a flock of birds: each star's motion across the sky and along our line of sight is measured, and stars moving in parallel at matching distances belong together. Five of the Dipper's stars pass, and their shared white follows from a shared age, since stars of similar weight born on the same day are still at the same stage of life.

NGC3532.question: Next to Carina's young clusters, what has time done to the Wishing Well's colors?
NGC3532.why: The Wishing Well lies a few degrees from the Carina Nebula, whose clusters are only a few million years old, so it lets you compare a young family with one many chapters further on.
NGC3532.look: From the Carina Nebula move about three degrees east-north-east to the big, rich oval of the Wishing Well. Look for its few yellow-orange stars among the white ones, then swing back toward the nebula's blue-white youngsters and compare.
NGC3532.answer: Time has taken its blue stars and left white ones and a few orange giants in charge, which is why the Wishing Well looks white and gold where the Carina clusters look blue. Its colors read a far later hour on the same clock, and a family's colors keep that time whether it lies near or far.
NGC3532.story: The Wishing Well's age is read from its brightest stars: the heaviest members still in their steady years mark how long the family has lived, because anything heavier has already swollen or died. Next to the young Carina clusters, whose blue-white giants still burn, that mark has slid far down to white stars, and the few orange giants are the members that have only just passed it.

IC2602.beat: A family still in its prime
IC2602.question: How young is a family whose brightest stars are all still blue-white?
IC2602.why: Around Theta Carinae spreads a naked-eye family of blue-white stars, the Southern Pleiades, and its uniform color is itself a clue to its age.
IC2602.look: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula, and take in the two or three dozen blue-white members around it. Hunt for a gold or orange star among the bright ones; there is none to find.
IC2602.answer: It is young enough that even its heaviest members are still in their steady adult lives, so none has swollen and reddened yet. That is the earliest face a family's color clock shows, all blue at the top, and every orange giant this family will ever have is still hidden among those blue-white stars.
IC2602.story: A family's top color works as a clock because its heaviest steady stars mark how long it has lived, and blue-white leaders mean even heavy stars have not had time to swell. Theta Carinae, at about 31,000 K, is in fact too hot for a family this old, so its history probably involves a partner, and astronomers time the family by its other members.

M47.question: Why does M47 sparkle while M46, in the same field, only glows?
M47.why: In Puppis two clusters share one binocular field, one coarse and bright, one fine and misty, and the difference between them shows what age and distance each do to a family's looks.
M47.look: Center M47, a coarse scatter of bright blue-white stars, then look just over a degree east for M46, a softer, finer, misty patch. Keep both in one field and compare their sparkle and texture.
M47.answer: Youth makes the sparkle, since M47 still keeps its heavy blue-white stars and each one stands out on its own. M46 has had about four times as long to lose its brightest members, so what is left melts into mist, a family whose clock has run long enough to take its own crown.
M47.story: Two clues are tangled in this field, because a cluster can look dim either by being far or by being old. Color pulls them apart: distance leaves a star's tint alone, so blue-white leaders in M47 mean heavy stars still in their steady years, while an older family's leaders have faded to plain white whatever its depth.

M46.question: M46 holds twice as many stars as M47; why does it look so much fainter?
M46.why: Beside bright M47 lies M46, a quiet glow that turns out to be the bigger family, which makes the pair a lesson in how little a cluster's looks say about its size.
M46.look: From M47 move just over a degree east. In 10×50 binoculars M46 is a soft, even glow with a few stars at the threshold; compare its total glow with M47's handful of bright stars.
M46.answer: Depth does much of the hiding, for M46 lies about three times farther than M47, and age does the rest by taking away the bright stars that would have stood out. Gaia finds nearly six times M47's mass in that modest glow, a family whose bulk now sits in small, faint, long-lived stars.
M46.story: A cluster's sparkle depends on its brightest few stars, not on its total count, and those few are the first to go as a family ages. That is why an old, rich cluster can look quieter than a young, poor one, and why astronomers count members with Gaia, star by star, rather than judging a family's size by its glitter.

NGC2451.question: NGC 2451 and NGC 2477 share a field; how different are the two families?
NGC2451.why: In Puppis a bold scatter of bright stars and a misty, grainy glow sit a degree and a half apart, and their contrast is as much about time as about distance.
NGC2451.look: Put the bright, scattered stars of NGC 2451, with orange c Puppis among them, at one side of the field and NGC 2477 at the other, a round, grainy haze. Compare sparkle with mist.
NGC2451.answer: NGC 2451 is young and near, about 26 million years old, while NGC 2477 is about 700 million years old and several times deeper, its blue stars long gone. Neighbors on the sky, they stand hundreds of millions of years apart on the clock that colors keep.
NGC2451.story: Color sorts these families where brightness cannot, since a far, rich cluster and a near, sparse one can glow alike. The bright stars of NGC 2451 are mostly blue-white, the hue of heavy stars still steady, while the leaders of NGC 2477 turned into giants long ago, too faint at that depth for binoculars to show their tint.

M44.question: The Beehive and the Hyades lie far apart in the sky; are they the same age?
M44.why: The Beehive is a swarm of white and pale-yellow stars with a few warmer ones among them, the color pattern of a family well into middle age, and it has a famous look-alike in Taurus.
M44.look: Midway between Pollux and Regulus, frame the Beehive and pick out its handful of yellow-orange giants among the white and pale-yellow stars. Notice that no bright blue-white star leads the swarm.
M44.answer: They are very nearly the same age, within a few tens of millions of years, and both show the same pattern of white stars joined by a few orange giants. Two families on opposite sides of the sky read the same hour on their clocks, which is just what you would expect if they were born in one great nursery and later drifted apart.
M44.story: Two families are dated alike when the same weight of star sits at the same turning point in both: the heaviest members still burning hydrogen in their cores, just below the few that have begun to swell. In the Beehive and the Hyades that turning point falls at about the same weight. The two also drift through space in nearly the same direction, part of why astronomers suspect a shared origin, though the case is not closed.

NGC6231.beat: A family at the very start
NGC6231.question: In a family only four million years old, has any star had time to age?
NGC6231.why: Half a degree north of the ζ pair in the Scorpion's tail lies NGC 6231, a tight knot of blue-white stars, and it shows a family at the very beginning of the clock that time writes in colors.
NGC6231.look: Follow the tail down to the naked-eye pair ζ¹ and ζ² Scorpii and go half a degree north to a compact knot of bright stars. They are almost all blue-white; compare them with orange ζ², a foreground star that does not belong.
NGC6231.answer: Only the very heaviest have begun to, and ζ¹ Scorpii, a member of about 36 times the Sun's mass, has already swollen into a hypergiant about a hundred times the Sun's width. Everyone else still blazes blue-white, so this family's clock has barely started, and yet its first stars are already in their last stage.
NGC6231.story: Stars of very different weights share the same blue-white color while they are young, so in a family this fresh the colors barely differ and the clock can be read only at its top end. There the heaviest stars, dozens of Suns each, burn through their core hydrogen in a few million years, faster than anything else in the sky.

M36.question: Three clusters in one sweep of Auriga; which is the youngest, and how can you tell?
M36.why: Auriga holds three star families in a single sweep, M36, M37 and M38, at broadly similar distances, so their differences in look are mostly differences in age.
M36.look: M36 is a small, compact knot with several bright stars popping out of it. Sweep about two and a half degrees north-west to M38 and about four degrees south-east to M37, and compare how much of each family's light sits in a few bright points.
M36.answer: M36 is the youngest, and its leaders are still hot blue-white stars, which is why it gathers into a small, bright knot. M38 is roughly twelve times older and M37 more than twenty, and in each the bright top has worn away, so the knot, the cloud and the fine grain are three readings of one clock.
M36.story: With the three families at similar distances, how bright their leading stars look is a fair comparison of how much light those stars truly give. That light climbs steeply with a star's weight, so the youngest family, which still has its heaviest members, puts most of its glow into a few bright points. As a family ages and loses those leaders, the same total light spreads across a crowd of fainter stars.

M37.question: Why does M37 look like fine sugar while M36 nearby is a bright, sparkling knot?
M37.why: M37 is the richest of Auriga's three star families, and set beside the young knot of M36 it shows what time does to a family's sparkle.
M37.look: From M36 move about four degrees east-south-east to M37, a round, rich, even glow with only a handful of stars resolved. Its stars are too faint to show color, so compare texture: M36's few bright sparks against M37's fine grain.
M37.answer: M37's heavy blue stars burned out long ago, and the light that remains comes from thousands of modest members blended together, with a few orange giants on top that only a telescope shows in color. The grain is age made visible: M37 has already spent the kind of star that still makes M36 glitter.
M37.story: In a young family the brightest stars are also the bluest, because the heaviest members are the hottest and the most luminous. Take those away and the brightest left are a few cool giants above a great many white and yellow stars of nearly equal brightness, too faint and too alike for any one of them to stand out at this distance. That is why age turns a cluster from sparks into grain, even when the older family holds more stars.

IC4756.question: IC 4756 and NGC 6633 look like twins; are they also alike in age?
IC4756.why: Across the border of Serpens and Ophiuchus two loose star families sit a few degrees apart, similar in size and brightness, a rare look-alike pair that might really be alike.
IC4756.look: From θ Serpentis sweep about four degrees west to IC 4756, a broad scatter of faint stars, then about three degrees farther west to NGC 6633, a longer, looser spray. Compare their looseness, and look for a yellowish point or two among the white; colors are faint at this brightness.
IC4756.answer: They are roughly alike, about 840 million years old for IC 4756 and 550 million for NGC 6633, at similar distances near 1,500 and 1,300 light-years. Their shared look is the honest one, two families whose clocks both stand at the hour when white stars begin, one by one, to swell into orange giants.
IC4756.story: Brightness and color can be taken at face value here because the two families sit at similar distances, so neither clue is bent by depth. Both have lost every blue-white star and are now led by a few swollen giants, the pattern of a family several hundred million years old. Gaia's parallaxes confirm that this time the matching looks are no trick of perspective.

M39.question: Why are M39's brightest stars all white, with no blue leaders among them?
M39.why: North-east of Deneb lies M39, a loose spray of stars shaped like a triangle, and the even white of its brightest members is the signature of a family that has already lost its heaviest.
M39.look: From Deneb sweep about 9° east-north-east to the loose triangle of M39. Count its brightest stars and judge their color: white or nearly so throughout, with no blazing blue leaders and no orange giants.
M39.answer: A family loses its stars from the heaviest down, so an all-white top puts M39 at a few hundred million years, however the models argue over the exact figure. Deneb, a short sweep away, is the kind of heavy star such a family burns through first, and it would have died long before M39's white stars ever change color.
M39.story: A family's brightest members are the heaviest it still has, so the color at the top of a cluster names the heaviest weight that has survived. Hot blue-white leaders mean stars many times the Sun's weight are still alive, and a white top means those are gone and the clock has reached stars of a few Suns. A yellow or orange top would mean that even those have begun to swell.

M41.question: Is M41's orange star a member of the family or a passer-by in front?
M41.why: M41 lies just south of Sirius, and near its middle one star glows orange among white ones, a color difference that could mean a sibling grown old or a stranger lined up.
M41.look: Put Sirius at the top of the field and move about four degrees south to M41. It breaks into dozens of stars, and near the middle one has a clear orange tint; compare it with the white stars around it.
M41.answer: It is family, a sibling that was born a little heavier and has already swollen into a giant while the others stay white. At about 150 million years only the heaviest members of M41 have made that change, so one orange star near the middle dates the whole cluster, much as a first gray hair dates a head.
M41.story: In a family of one age, a small difference in birth weight makes a large difference in pace, so the line between steady stars and swollen ones is sharp. The giants of M41 began only a little heavier than its brightest white stars, yet they have already crossed into old age while those just below the line look untouched.

M67.question: M67 and the Beehive share Cancer; why does M67 look like a faint mist?
M67.why: Cancer holds two star families, the bright Beehive and the faint M67, and between them they span much of the life of an open cluster.
M67.look: From Acubens, the star at the bottom of Cancer about nine degrees south of the Beehive, drift about two degrees west to M67, a small, faint, grainy glow. No color shows at this brightness, so compare its texture with the Beehive's bright, scattered stars.
M67.answer: M67 is about six times the Beehive's age, so only Sun-like stars and a few giants remain, and it also lies more than four times farther away. Age and distance together turn a rich family into a faint mist, and its brightest giants show what the Sun itself will one day become.
M67.story: Both clues are needed to untangle this one, because M67 is older and also farther away than the Beehive, and either alone could dim a family. Distance only shrinks and fades the view, leaving each star's true power as it was, while age removes the most powerful stars altogether. With Gaia fixing the distance, the faintness left over is age: the stars at M67's turning point are only slightly heavier than the Sun.

HR6165.question: Antares and τ Scorpii were born in one family; why do they look so unlike?
HR6165.why: τ Scorpii is a plain blue-white point a couple of degrees from Antares, and both belong to the young family of Upper Scorpius, which turns their contrast into a story about weight rather than age.
HR6165.look: Put Antares at one edge of a wide field and sweep about two degrees south-east to τ Scorpii. Swing back and forth, deep orange against crisp blue-white, and defocus slightly to judge the colors as small disks.
HR6165.answer: Born about 11 million years ago in the same family, Antares started out the heavier, perhaps 15 Suns, and has already swollen into a red supergiant while τ still burns quietly as a compact blue star. That span is a blink in the life of a star like the Sun, so a family this young already split into red and blue shows how hard weight presses on the clock.
HR6165.story: Antares almost certainly once looked much like τ, a compact blue-white star burning hydrogen in its core. When that core ran dry it shrank and heated, the layers above it ballooned outward, and as the surface spread it cooled, so the color slid from blue-white toward red. Here color is the record of a swelling, which is why the thermometer and the size measurement tell the same story.

NGC2516.question: Can a family's colors give its age even when distance dims every star?
NGC2516.why: The Southern Beehive, beside the False Cross in Carina, is a family born about when the Pleiades were but set much deeper in space, a natural test of which clue survives the distance.
NGC2516.look: From Avior, the orange corner of the False Cross, move about three degrees west. Binoculars show dozens of stars in a patch the width of the full Moon, mostly white and blue-white, with the brightest in a rough box and none of them dazzling.
NGC2516.answer: Its colors give the age undimmed, because the hottest stars a family still holds depend on time, not on where you stand. The Southern Beehive keeps blue-white stars at its top, the look of a family the Pleiades' age, and its light has carried that date across the extra distance as faithfully as a postmark.
NGC2516.story: Distance drains brightness but leaves color alone, so a family's colors read the same hour near or far. The Southern Beehive's brightest steady stars are blue-white, the same top color as in the Pleiades, and that matching hand on the clock is how two families so differently placed can be seen to share an age.
